title: Low-Cost Soil Moisture Sensing for Smallholder Irrigation

headings.text: Low-Cost Soil Moisture Sensing for Smallholder Irrigation

key_sentences: Prepared by the Field Systems Group of the Department of Agricultural Engineering.
Smallholder farmers often irrigate on a fixed calendar because commercial soil moisture sensors cost more than a season's income from a small plot.
Over one growing season it stayed within 2.5 percent of a reference neutron probe.
Cheaper sensors exist, but their readings drift as the probe corrodes in wet soil.
The coated probes stayed within 2.5 percent of the reference throughout the season.
A coated probe costing under five dollars is accurate enough to schedule irrigation for smallholders.
Field trials with 200 farms will start in March 2027.
This work was supported by the Eastbrook Rural Futures Fund.

tables.caption: Table 1. Error against the reference probe

list_items.text: 1. Probes were buried at 15 cm and 30 cm depth in four plots.
2. Readings were logged every hour by a battery-powered board.
3. Each probe was recalibrated against soil cores every four weeks.
• Coating cut drift from 3.1 to 0.4 percent per month.
• The probes survived a full season without failures.
• Cost per sensor was 7 percent of the commercial unit.
Test in sandy and clay soils.
[1] Field Systems Group (2024). Annual report on sensor drift. Eastbrook University Press.
[2] Irrigation Standards Board (2021). Guidelines for soil moisture measurement, second edition.
[3] Agri-Tech Research Day (2025). Proceedings of the poster session on low-cost instrumentation.
